lines.text: Your microwave heats food with no flame and no hot coil. Instead, it shakes the water inside your food.
A part called a magnetron turns electricity into microwaves, radio waves about twelve centimeters long.
Water molecules are slightly positive at one end and negative at the other.
The microwave's electric field swings back and forth two point four five billion times a second, and the molecules twist to follow it.
All that jostling turns into heat. But the waves only reach about a centimeter in. The middle warms up from the outside.
The waves also pile up into hot and cold spots. That's why your plate spins.
And the door? Its metal mesh has holes far smaller than the waves, so they bounce back, but light slips through.
